note: Claims that span areas, or sit in files the other groups do not own.

assertions.claim: The pinned core surface is 122 Core/*.cs files, byte-identical across SDKs modulo the root namespace.
assertions.defends: the core-surface stamp at the top of dotnet-authentication, -calling-endpoints, -client-initialization, -configuration-resilience and -models

assertions.claim: This surface has no Core/Models/AdditionalProperties.cs — that file is one of the three the current codegen-v2 template adds, and its presence means the SDK in hand is a LATER surface than the skills describe.
assertions.defends: the core-surface stamp — 'it adds Hooks/SdkHook.cs, Models/AdditionalProperties.cs and Extensions/HttpContentExtensions.cs'

assertions.claim: This surface has no Core/Extensions/HttpContentExtensions.cs — the third of the three codegen-v2 template additions the stamp names.
assertions.defends: the core-surface stamp — 'it adds Hooks/SdkHook.cs, Models/AdditionalProperties.cs and Extensions/HttpContentExtensions.cs'

assertions.claim: Pageable<TPage,TItem> is a public type in {RootNamespace}.Core.Pagination.
assertions.defends: dotnet-configuration-resilience § Pagination — the type a paginated operation returns

assertions.claim: Pageable<TPage, TItem> implements IAsyncEnumerable<TItem>, so a plain await foreach walks individual items, not pages.
assertions.defends: dotnet-configuration-resilience § Pagination — 'the shape catches people out'

assertions.claim: AsPages(ct) is a public method on Pageable returning IAsyncEnumerable<TPage> — the page, not the item — and its cancellation token is optional.
assertions.defends: dotnet-configuration-resilience § Pagination — 'When you want the page rather than the items, call .AsPages(ct)'

assertions.claim: The SDK advances the paging state for you — offset, cursor, Link-header or page-number, depending on the operation. (The generator emits FIVE IPageState implementations; the fifth, keyset, is not in the skill's list.)
assertions.defends: dotnet-configuration-resilience § Pagination — '(offset, cursor, `Link`-header, or page-number, depending on the operation)'

assertions.claim: A streaming operation's response mapper produces IAsyncEnumerable<{Item}> — which is what makes the generated signature Task<IAsyncEnumerable<{Item}>>: awaited once to open the stream, then enumerated frame by frame.
assertions.defends: dotnet-configuration-resilience § Streaming (Server-Sent Events)

assertions.claim: {Item} is `string` for a plain-text stream — the plain-text factory fixes the item type to string, while the JSON factory deserializes each frame into the typed model.
assertions.defends: dotnet-configuration-resilience § Streaming — '{Item} is string for a plain-text stream, or a typed model for a JSON event stream'

assertions.claim: The idle window is a TimeSpan? carried on the SSE response itself and defaults to NONE — every generated SSE factory declares `idleTimeout = null`, so unless an operation opts in there is no idle-timeout check at all.
assertions.defends: dotnet-configuration-resilience § Streaming, Idle timeout — 'the idle window is a TimeSpan? carried on the SSE response itself, defaulting to none'

assertions.claim: A path/query parameter's value is normalised *through* JSON before substitution — the scalar is serialized and re-parsed, so a DateTimeOffset or a generated enum goes on the wire in its JSON form, not whatever ToString() would give.
assertions.defends: dotnet-configuration-resilience § Verify on the wire — 'it is normalised through JSON'

assertions.claim: The path-parameter flattener switches on the JSON-normalised value, not on the raw object — which is what puts the normalisation on the path-substitution route and not just on request bodies.
assertions.defends: dotnet-configuration-resilience § Verify on the wire — 'it is normalised through JSON'

assertions.pattern: /// <exception cref="SdkException\{TResult\}"> of <see cref="\w+"/> when the server returns an error response\.</exception>
assertions.claim: The operation's XML doc carries an <exception> line naming the TError — the fact 'lives in the method's XML doc <exception> line', so it is readable on hover without opening the error class.
assertions.defends: dotnet-error-handling § Which TError does an endpoint throw? — 'In the source itself the same fact lives in the method's XML doc <exception> line'

assertions.claim: `SdkException{TResult}` is boilerplate — identical on every method — so it is NOT the type you catch; {TResult} is the doc comment's generic placeholder.
assertions.defends: dotnet-error-handling § Which TError does an endpoint throw?

assertions.pattern: exception cref="SdkException\{TResult\}">(?! of <see cref="\w+"/> when the server returns an error response\.</exception>)
assertions.claim: The operation's XML doc <exception> line has a fixed shape — `<exception cref="SdkException{TResult}"> of <see cref="…"/> when the server returns an error response.</exception>` — so the type named after `of <see cref=` is always where the actual TError is read from.
assertions.defends: dotnet-error-handling § Which TError does an endpoint throw? — 'The type named after of <see cref="…"/> is the actual TError'

assertions.claim: A non-2xx response throws: success is the spec-derived allowlist when one is configured, otherwise the 200-299 default — so 304 is NOT success.
assertions.defends: dotnet-calling-endpoints § Making the call and reading the response; dotnet-testing § Test a success path

assertions.claim: The generated client constructs the status policy with an EMPTY success allowlist — which is the condition under which 'a non-2xx response throws' is literally exact. A fixture that emits a spec-derived allowlist would need the sentence reworded to 'outside the operation's success set'.
assertions.defends: dotnet-calling-endpoints § Making the call and reading the response — 'a non-2xx response throws, it is not signalled by the return value'

assertions.claim: OnRetry receives a RetryAttempt carrying AttemptNumber, Delay and Reason — the three members the skill's OnRetry sample reads.
assertions.defends: dotnet-configuration-resilience § Retries — the OnRetry sample and 'OnRetry's RetryAttempt also carries Reason'

assertions.claim: RetryAttempt.Reason is either RetryReason.Status(HttpStatusCode) or RetryReason.Failure(Exception) — the SDK itself distinguishes a status fault from a transport fault.
assertions.defends: dotnet-configuration-resilience § Retries — 'RetryReason.Status(HttpStatusCode) or RetryReason.Failure(Exception)'; dotnet-testing § Notes

assertions.claim: RetryReason's constructor is private, so the two cases are the whole hierarchy — nothing outside the file can add a third, and a switch over Status and Failure is exhaustive.
assertions.defends: dotnet-configuration-resilience § Retries — 'RetryReason.Status(HttpStatusCode) or RetryReason.Failure(Exception)'

assertions.claim: Each controller property on the client is named exactly for its controller type, which is what makes `client.{ApiGroup}.{Operation}(...)` resolve with {ApiGroup} read straight off the Api/ class name.
assertions.defends: dotnet-client-initialization § Shape of the client — 'grouped under controller properties (one per API resource group) and called client.{ApiGroup}.{Operation}(...)'

assertions.claim: Where an operation carries a JSON request body, the parameter holding it is named `body` — so the request type is the type of the operation's `body` parameter.
assertions.defends: dotnet-calling-endpoints § Building request models — 'The request type is the type of the operation's body parameter'

assertions.claim: Methods are async-only (no sync overloads) — every public member of a generated controller returns Task (or Pageable for a paginated operation).
assertions.defends: dotnet-calling-endpoints § Method signature convention — 'Methods are async-only (no sync overloads)'

assertions.claim: Where a model has no additional-properties map, unknown JSON fields are DROPPED on deserialization — nothing in the SDK sets UnmappedMemberHandling.Disallow, so a field the model does not declare can never make a response throw.
assertions.defends: dotnet-models § Unknown / future fields — 'unknown fields are dropped on deserialization'

assertions.claim: The only place a date converter can be injected is the response mapper's optional converter argument, and it is registered on the JsonSerializerOptions for the WHOLE payload — which is why the four date converters attach to whole-response payloads and never to a property inside a model.
assertions.defends: dotnet-models § Dates & numbers — 'it attaches them to whole-response payloads … not to properties inside a model'

assertions.claim: Set credentials BEFORE constructing the client: the scheme captures the credentials value in a constant closure when the client's constructor builds AuthSchemes, so assigning the options property afterwards is never observed.
assertions.defends: dotnet-authentication § Notes — 'Set credentials before constructing the client'

assertions.claim: A grant strategy is built through one of exactly two token-request factories — ForBasicAuthRequest or ForFormBodyRequest — so 'check which factory your generated AuthSchemes uses' is a two-way choice, not an open set.
assertions.defends: dotnet-authentication § OAuth 2.0 — authorization code, the ClientSecret table — 'Check which factory your generated AuthSchemes uses before treating the secret as optional'

assertions.claim: All three OAuth2 grants (client-credentials, authorization-code, resource-owner-password) expose both token-request factories — six in total — so the basic-vs-form-body choice, and the client-secret rule that hangs off it, applies to every grant.
assertions.defends: dotnet-authentication § OAuth 2.0 — authorization code, the ClientSecret table
